Neonatal body mass in the Mountain hare (Lepus timidus) has been documented at approximately 107.93 grams [Wwb = approximately 107.93 grams], a value consistent with the precocial developmental strategy typical of leporids. Newborn leverets are fully furred and have their eyes open at birth, allowing them to become mobile within hours of parturition. This initial mass, while modest, is sufficient to support the rapid growth trajectory that characterizes the early life stages of this species. The wet weight at birth is a critical determinant of early survival, particularly in the harsh alpine and tundra environments that L. timidus inhabits across its Palearctic range. Field studies indicate that neonates born with lower body masses experience reduced thermoregulatory capacity during the critical first days of life, when exposure to cold stress is greatest. The ability to achieve a birth mass of this magnitude is linked to maternal body condition during gestation, with females that occupy high-quality habitats typically producing offspring that fall within the upper range of reported values. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Lepus europaeus reveal a similar birth mass, suggesting a conserved evolutionary constraint on neonatal size within the genus. In contrast, the much larger Lepus arcticus, a close relative of the mountain hare, shows a slightly higher neonatal mass, reflecting its adaptation to even more extreme Arctic conditions. Understanding these subtle interspecific differences provides insight into the selective pressures shaping life-history variation in high-latitude lagomorphs.

Females of Lepus timidus typically produce two pups per litter [N_R_i = two pups per litter], a reproductive output that aligns with the moderate fecundity observed across boreal and montane hare species. The frequency of reproductive events is approximately 2 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 litters per year], resulting in a substantial annual reproductive effort. This combination of a modest per-litter output with a relatively high yearly frequency means that a single female can produce upwards of four leverets over the course of a single breeding season, enabling population persistence despite significant predation pressure from foxes, raptors, and mustelids. This core body temperature is maintained through a combination of pelage insulation and behavioral thermoregulation, even when ambient temperatures fall well below freezing. Gestation in the mountain hare lasts a total of 50 days [tg = 50 days] when measured at the species’ typical core body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. The weaning process is gradual, with young hares beginning to sample solid vegetation as early as two weeks of age while continuing to suckle intermittently. The age at weaning is a critical life-history transition because it marks the point at which juveniles must meet all their energetic requirements through foraging, a challenging endeavor in the resource-limited landscapes of the subarctic and alpine habitats they occupy. Survival rates during the post-weaning period are highly variable, influenced by the quality of the early summer forage and the timing of the first major snowfall. The relatively short nursing period reflects the precocial nature of hare neonates, which are capable of ingesting solid food at an early age compared to altricial mammals that require extended parental care.

This age at puberty, measured at a core body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], positions the mountain hare as a relatively fast-maturing species among mammals of comparable body size. The attainment of reproductive capability at roughly nine months of age means that individuals born early in the year are able to contribute to the breeding population during the subsequent reproductive season. This early maturation is an adaptive response to high extrinsic mortality rates, allowing at least a subset of the cohort to reproduce before being removed by predation or environmental extremes. The onset of gonadal activity is triggered by increasing day length following the winter solstice, and females exhibit their first estrus shortly after the snowmelt, typically in March or April at lower latitudes and somewhat later in the Arctic. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult Mountain hare has been reported at 4175 grams [Wwi = 4175 grams], a figure that places this species among the medium-sized members of the genus Lepus. This maximum body mass is typically attained by individuals in their second year of life, following the completion of skeletal growth and the accumulation of sufficient fat reserves to survive the winter. Body mass shows considerable seasonal variation, with individuals being heaviest in autumn as they prepare for the cold months and lightest in late spring after the energetic demands of the breeding season. The maximum recorded longevity for this species in the wild is approximately 18 years [am = approximately 18 years], measured against its core body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], although most individuals in natural populations rarely survive beyond four or five years due to predation and environmental stressors. Such a potential lifespan is unusually long for a mammal of this body size and reflects the species' evolutionary history in stable but resource-poor environments where delayed senescence can be advantageous. Comparative analyses across the family Leporidae suggest that the mountain hare’s extended lifespan is linked to its relatively slow metabolic rate and its capacity for seasonal torpor-like energy conservation, both of which reduce cumulative oxidative damage over time. The interplay between a sizable adult body mass and a long potential lifespan creates a life-history strategy that balances relatively high fecundity against the need for somatic durability in a challenging environment.
